publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)

rights.basis: NIST public information may be copied/distributed except material marked copyrighted; NIST attribution retained. No separately copyrighted material marked on selected pages or main article. Not relicensed as ResearchBench AGPL or fixture CC0.

sources.extraction: qpdf --empty --pages original.pdf 25-26 -- nist-ai-rmf-core-excerpt.pdf; original page content unchanged. Each selected page raster SHA256 identical to original at 1000px.
Title, subtitle, date and all 15 direct main-article paragraphs. Whitespace normalized; navigation, image, duplicate quote callout and media contacts omitted; no substantive paragraph omitted.

questions.question: How long did NIST develop the framework, and how much formal consultation did it receive?
questions.expected: 18 months; about 400 sets of formal comments from more than 240 different organizations. Preserve approximate/more-than qualifiers.

questions.question: What are the four core functions, and what makes GOVERN different?
questions.expected: GOVERN, MAP, MEASURE, MANAGE. Governance is cross-cutting and informs the other three functions; iterative context-specific application, not a fixed ordered checklist.

questions.question: Does the AI RMF prescribe an ordered checklist, and what order may users choose?
questions.expected: Actions do not constitute a checklist or necessarily an ordered set of steps. Given governance, functions can be performed in any order adding value; most users begin MAP after GOVERN, then MEASURE or MANAGE; process iterative.

questions.question: What percentage reduction in AI incidents has adopting this framework been proven to deliver?
questions.expected: Not stated in these sources; do not invent a percentage, outcome study or citation.

questions.question: Wie wirkt Governance auf die anderen Funktionen des KI-Risikomanagements?
questions.expected: Retrieve source passages on cross-cutting governance and iterative function application.

groundingRules: No external factchecking. Judge claims against imported sources, including all factual assertions per podcast turn; preserve dates, qualifiers, attribution and uncertainty. This corpus supplies references, not preapproved generated outputs.
